What happens: Single-name holders have an empty surname field; MRZ reads '<<GIVEN'. Systems that require a last name insert FNU, repeat the given name, or add an initial.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Filler and duplicated tokens match unrelated WC records and inflate scores.
Recommended control: Allow a null surname; strip FNU/LNU/duplicate tokens before screening; screen on the MRZ secondary identifier.

What happens: South Indian convention uses the father's initial (R. Keerthana); the passport expands it into a surname.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: CRM name collapses to one strong token, so it matches any WC subject with that given name.
Recommended control: Expand initials from the passport; keep the initial form as an AKA.

What happens: Same name romanised differently across documents (Chaudhary/Choudhary/Chowdhury; Mohammed/Mohammad).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Exact matching misses true hits; loose fuzzy matching floods alerts.
Recommended control: Adopt passport spelling as legal name; phonetic rules tuned for Indic transliteration; store variants as AKAs.

What happens: Passport not reissued after marriage while Aadhaar/PAN show the married surname (or the reverse).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: One surname is never screened on its own; WC may list the person under either.
Recommended control: Collect marriage certificate; screen both surnames; store former name.

What happens: Maharashtra/Gujarat passports carry the father's name in given names (SAGAR VIJAY PATIL; CHIRAG RAMESHBHAI PATEL); Gujarati documents often lead with the surname.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Parsers make the father's name the first name or drop it, removing a discriminator.
Recommended control: Map fields from the passport; keep father's name as middle name and use it to discount hits.

What happens: Surname keyed into the first-name field at onboarding.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Order-weighted engines under-score the true name; a real hit may only appear on re-screen.
Recommended control: Rebuild fields from MRZ primary/secondary identifiers; order-insensitive matching.

What happens: Titles (Smt., Shri, Dr.) and abbreviations (Mohd., Md.) copied from bills or PAN into CRM.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Extra tokens distort similarity and cross-match other abbreviated records.
Recommended control: Honorific stop-list; dictionary expansion of abbreviations before screening.

What happens: Telugu names lead with a house name and carry 3–5 given names, often shortened to initials (V V S R K Prasad).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Only one full token survives, so generic matches spike.
Recommended control: Screen the full VIZ name; expand initials; tag house name as surname.

What happens: CRM holds Bill/Bob/Liz instead of William/Robert/Elizabeth.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: A true WC hit on the legal name can be missed entirely.
Recommended control: Screen the passport legal name; nickname dictionary; preferred name stored as AKA.

Variance Type: Middle name vs initial vs omitted
What happens: Full middle name on passport, initial on driver's license, nothing in CRM.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: The middle name is often the only name-level discriminator against same-name subjects.
Recommended control: Carry the full middle name into screening; use it to discount.

What happens: Suffix on the passport but dropped by the license or CRM.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Father and son share name and address history; WC hits on the other generation.
Recommended control: Dedicated suffix field; DOB to separate generations.

What happens: Hispanic double surnames (GARCIA-LOPEZ) split, merged or truncated; MRZ turns the hyphen into a filler.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Screening on one component misses WC records filed under the full or other component.
Recommended control: Screen full, paternal-only and maternal-only permutations; treat hyphen and space as equal.

What happens: Passport still in maiden name; license and CRM in married name.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Maiden surname never screened; WC may list the subject under it.
Recommended control: Marriage certificate; former name as AKA and screened.

What happens: O'Brien, McDonald, De La Cruz, St. Clair written with and without punctuation or spaces (MRZ drops apostrophes).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Tokenisers split or merge the prefix differently, depressing scores.
Recommended control: Punctuation-insensitive comparison; prefix-joining rules.

What happens: Names longer than the 39-character MRZ field are truncated; OCR onboarding copies the truncated MRZ into CRM.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Lost tokens lower scores against WC records holding the full name.
Recommended control: Use the visual-zone name as source of truth; MRZ only for document checks.

What happens: Vietnamese and Indian-born citizens appear in US order or under an anglicised / short name (Tony for Tuấn, Srini for Venkata Srinivas).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: WC records in the origin-country format are missed or under-scored.
Recommended control: Store former name from the naturalization certificate; screen in both orders.

What happens: Online forms push Western order (An Van Nguyen) or store the family name in the first-name field.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Engines treat the given name as the surname; true hits score low.
Recommended control: Map family name from the MRZ primary identifier; screen both orders.

What happens: MRZ and many CRMs hold ASCII; legacy interfaces turn UTF-8 into mojibake (Nguyá»…n).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Corrupted names produce no usable tokens; stripped names lose distinguishing tone marks.
Recommended control: Store Vietnamese-script and ASCII forms; fix interface encoding; repair from the ID card.

What happens: Đ appears as D (MRZ), Đ (ID card), 'Dd' (Telex typing), 'Dj' (legacy) or the look-alike Ð (U+00D0).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Byte-level mismatches block exact and fuzzy matches.
Recommended control: Normalise Đ/Ð/Dd/Dj → D for matching only.

What happens: Different names (Hùng/Hưng, Hương/Hường, Linh/Lĩnh) fold to the same ASCII string.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Two different people look like an exact match; false-positive volume rises.
Recommended control: Unicode-aware comparison against WC native-script names.

What happens: CRM keeps only family + last given name (Nguyen Huong) or merges compound names (Thanhhuong).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Shortened names match many more WC profiles; merged names match none.
Recommended control: Restore the full VIZ name; keep compound tokens separate.

What happens: Nguyễn, Trần and Lê cover over half the population, so full-name duplicates are common.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: One customer can return several WC profiles; alert volume dominates analyst time.
Recommended control: Discount on DOB, ID-card number and place of birth; good-guy list.

What happens: Vietnamese women keep their birth family name; forms built for Western naming prompt a husband's surname.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: The legal name is never screened.
Recommended control: Restore passport name; married name as AKA; fix form guidance.

What happens: Passport address page reflects the address at issue; customers move and update only Aadhaar.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Address-based discounting compares against a stale city.
Recommended control: Use Aadhaar e-KYC or recent utility bill for current address; passport as identity only.

What happens: Bangalore/Bengaluru, Gurgaon/Gurugram, Bombay/Mumbai, Allahabad/Prayagraj in different documents.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: City token mismatch blocks auto-matching.
Recommended control: City alias table; anchor on PIN code.

What happens: Aadhaar addresses begin with S/O, D/O, W/O, C/O and include 'Near …' landmarks.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Token overlap with CRM falls below threshold.
Recommended control: Strip relationship prefixes and landmark phrases; match on PIN + locality.

What happens: PIN keyed with transposed or wrong digits.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Same address fails to match; wrong delivery area for checks.
Recommended control: Validate PIN against the India Post directory.

What happens: Non-resident Indians live abroad but documents carry an Indian permanent address.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Two jurisdictions appear to conflict when compared with WC.
Recommended control: Record overseas (current) and Indian (permanent) addresses separately; compare WC against both.

What happens: B-302, B/302, Flat No. 302 B-Wing, 302-B.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Unit tokens do not align.
Recommended control: Parse wing and flat number into separate fields.

What happens: Aadhaar uses the revenue district (Gautam Buddha Nagar, SAS Nagar) where others use the city (Noida, Mohali).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: City mismatch on an identical address.
Recommended control: District-to-city crosswalk; PIN anchor.

Variance Type: No address on passport – stale DL address
What happens: US passports carry no address; the driver's license used as proof is often out of date.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Current residence cannot be evidenced from ID documents.
Recommended control: Accept recent utility bill / bank statement for CIP; prompt license update.

What happens: Street vs St, Apartment vs Apt vs #, North vs N.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: String comparison fails on identical addresses.
Recommended control: USPS CASS standardisation before comparison.

What happens: ZIP+4 on one record, 5-digit ZIP on another, or transposed digits.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Exact-match comparison fails.
Recommended control: Validate ZIP; compare on 5 digits.

What happens: Customer gives a PO Box as residential address.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Not acceptable as residential address under CIP; no match to documents.
Recommended control: Capture street address; keep PO Box as mailing.

What happens: Manhattan/New York, Hollywood/Los Angeles, Little Saigon/Westminster.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: City mismatch on an identical address.
Recommended control: USPS preferred-city lookup by ZIP.

What happens: Service members use APO/FPO addresses; license shows home of record.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Two addresses appear to conflict.
Recommended control: Accept APO/FPO; store home of record as secondary.

What happens: Winter address in FL/AZ in CRM; primary residence elsewhere on the license.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Residence and jurisdiction unclear.
Recommended control: Determine primary residence; store seasonal address as alternate.

What happens: ID cards issued before July 2025 show district-level units and pre-merger provinces (e.g. Bình Dương, now part of TP. Hồ Chí Minh).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Old and new addresses for the same home do not match.
Recommended control: Pre-/post-reform administrative-unit crosswalk; store both versions.

What happens: ID card shows hometown permanent residence (thường trú); customer actually lives in a city under temporary residence (tạm trú).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: ID address and actual residence are in different provinces.
Recommended control: Form CT07 residence confirmation; record both addresses.

What happens: Full Vietnamese, abbreviations (P., Q., TP.HCM) and English translations (Ward 7, District 3) for one address.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: String comparison fails on identical addresses.
Recommended control: Abbreviation dictionary; Vietnamese↔English unit mapping; diacritic folding for comparison.

What happens: Alley addresses written with slashes in different orders (45/12/3 vs Số 3, Hẻm 45/12).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: House and alley numbers are mis-parsed.
Recommended control: Alley-aware parser; adopt ID-card form.

What happens: Quận 2 → TP. Thủ Đức (2021, itself dissolved in 2025); Thừa Thiên Huế → TP. Huế (2025).
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Old and new names for the same place do not match.
Recommended control: Historical place-name table.

What happens: Vietnamese nationals abroad keep a Vietnamese permanent address on the ID card.
Why it hurts screening / KYC: Two countries appear to conflict.
Recommended control: Record overseas address as residential and Vietnamese address as permanent.
